title: Effect of screening mammography on the risk of breast cancer deaths and of all-cause deaths: a systematic review with meta-analysis of cohort studies
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies
population: Women attending versus not attending mammography screening in 13 cohort studies
evidence_excerpt: The random-effects summary relative risk for breast cancer mortality in screening attendees versus nonattendees was 0.55 (95% CI 0.50-0.60) across 13 cohort studies.
limitations: Screening attendees and nonattendees may differ in baseline risk and health behavior.
Relative risk cannot be converted to lives saved per 1,000 without baseline mortality and a time horizon.

title: Effect of mammographic screening from age 40 years on breast cancer mortality (UK Age trial): final results of a randomised, controlled trial
population: Women beginning annual mammography at age 40 or 41
intervention: Annual mammography beginning at age 40 or 41
comparator: Standard care without screening before the national program invitation
time_horizon: First ten years and later follow-up
evidence_excerpt: The authors reported a relative reduction in breast cancer mortality during the first ten years, with attenuation thereafter while the absolute reduction remained constant.
evidence_strength: Randomized trial; numeric effect absent from demo abstract
limitations: The fixed demo abstract does not contain a numeric effect estimate.
The population beginning screening at age 40 or 41 may not represent all women aged 40-74.

title: Effect of organised mammography screening on stage-specific incidence in Norway: population study
population: Women eligible for organized screening compared with younger ineligible women
comparator: Concurrent changes among younger women ineligible for screening
evidence_excerpt: Screening introduction was followed by increased localised incidence and no change in advanced-stage incidence relative to the comparison group.
limitations: The abstract does not report a transferable stage-shift percentage.
Advanced-stage incidence did not decline in the reported comparison.
